hints: Differentiate \(f(x)=\cos x/(1+\sin x)\) using the quotient rule.
Use \(\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1\) to simplify the numerator completely.
On \(-\tfrac\pi2<x<\tfrac{3\pi}2\), use \(\sin x>-1\) to show \(1+\sin x>0\), so the simplified derivative is negative throughout.
walkthrough:
State the given function:
$$f(x) = \dfrac{\cos x}{1 + \sin x}$$

Differentiate $f(x)$ using the quotient rule $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$:
Let $u = \cos x \implies u' = -\sin x$.
Let $v = 1 + \sin x \implies v' = \cos x$.

Substitute these into the quotient rule formula:
$$f'(x) = \dfrac{(-\sin x)(1 + \sin x) - (\cos x)(\cos x)}{(1 + \sin x)^2}$$

Expand the terms in the numerator:
$$(-\sin x)(1 + \sin x) - \cos^2 x = -\sin x - \sin^2 x - \cos^2 x = -\sin x - (\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x)$$

Apply the Pythagorean identity $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$:
$$- \sin x - (\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x) = -\sin x - 1 = -(1 + \sin x)$$

Substitute the simplified numerator back into the derivative:
$$f'(x) = \dfrac{-(1 + \sin x)}{(1 + \sin x)^2}$$

Cancel the common factor $(1 + \sin x)$ between numerator and denominator:
$$f'(x) = -\dfrac{1}{1 + \sin x}$$

Analyze the sign of $f'(x)$ on the interval $-\dfrac{1}{2}\pi < x < \dfrac{1}{2}\pi$:
For all $x$ in $-\dfrac{1}{2}\pi < x < \dfrac{1}{2}\pi$, the sine function satisfies $-1 < \sin x < 1$.
Therefore, $1 + \sin x > 1 + (-1) = 0$.
Since the denominator $(1 + \sin x)$ is strictly positive and the numerator is $-1$, the fraction is strictly negative:
$$f'(x) = -\dfrac{1}{1 + \sin x} < 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\pi, \dfrac{1}{2}\pi\right)$$

hints: Use the substitution pattern \(u=1+\sin x\), since \(du=\cos x\,dx\).
The antiderivative is therefore logarithmic; evaluate it at \(\pi/2\) and \(\pi/6\).
Combine the difference of logarithms into one simplified exact logarithm.
walkthrough:
State the given definite integral:
$$I = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\cos x}{1 + \sin x}\,dx$$

Recognise that the numerator is the exact derivative of the denominator: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(1 + \sin x) = \cos x$.
Alternatively, use the substitution $u = 1 + \sin x \implies du = \cos x\,dx$.

Transform the limits of integration:
When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $u = 1 + \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2}$.
When $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $u = 1 + \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 1 + 1 = 2$.

Rewrite the integral in terms of $u$:
$$I = \int_{3/2}^2 \dfrac{1}{u}\,du = \left[ \ln|u| \right]_{3/2}^2$$

Apply the quotient rule of logarithms $\ln a - \ln b = \ln\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)$:
$$I = \ln\left( \dfrac{2}{3/2} \right) = \ln\left( 2 \times \dfrac{2}{3} \right) = \ln\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)$$
